events.desc: The library. My library — or it should have been. The tall ceilings press down like the inside of a skull, and the inscription on the mantelpiece pulls at something older than strategy.
events.thinking:
Alone. The library door settles into its frame behind me and something in my face releases — not a muscle I can name, but the held quality around the eyes, the warmth kept ready at the corners of the mouth. Pemberton's face. It falls away the way a coat falls from a hook when no one is wearing it. My ears hold the corridor for two full seconds before the rest of me believes the silence.

**My shoulders settle into a different alignment** — wider, claiming more of the doorframe than Pemberton would allow. My spine finds its full height and stays there, not reaching, not performing — arrived. My feet plant into the floor with a weight that has nothing to do with standing and everything to do with owning. The tall ceilings press down and my body presses back, filling the vertical the way water fills a glass. This room should organise around me. It does. Beneath the settling, my hearing reads the house — the tick of the hallway clock, a floorboard shifting in the east wing, the specific quality of silence that means no one is on the stairs. The monitoring never fully switches off. It runs underneath the ownership the way plumbing runs underneath a floor.

**My hands find the book spines before my eyes have finished adjusting to the light.** The leather is cool and cracked under my fingertips — each title a memory stored in the pads of my fingers rather than in any catalogue. I built these shelves. I chose which spines face outward, which authors greet visitors, which volumes hide behind the front row where only my hands would find them. My fingertips move along the ridge of the third shelf and the body's inventory is faster than thought — Montaigne, then the gap where the Trollope was before I moved it, then the law volumes I positioned so Clara would never browse past them. Every placement a decision. Every decision still holding after twenty years. The dust settles into the grooves my palms have worn into the shelf edges.

**The inscription on the mantelpiece sharpens.** Everything else dims — the leather chairs, the dust motes spiralling in the window light, the shelves I was just touching. My attention narrows to the carved stone the way a lens narrows light, peripheral vision collapsing until there is only the lettering and the slight acceleration in my pulse. My fingertips leave the shelf and my body moves toward the fireplace without deciding to. The stone is cold under my hand. The letters are worn but legible, and something in my chest opens — not the spine's territorial weight, not the body's ownership of shelves and spines, but a quickening behind the breastbone where the first thread of a plan becomes visible. Time compresses around the reading. My hands are steady. My breathing is shallow and even, the way it gets when every detail matters and the body knows it before the mind has caught up.

**Behind my sternum, warmth pools** — slow, heavy, spreading outward into my shoulders until they drop another fraction of an inch. The private heat of a room that answers only to me. Every shelf I built, every book I placed, every late night cataloguing the estate's holdings while the house slept — all of it settling into a sweetness that has nothing to do with the inscription and everything to do with standing here, in this room, where twenty years of my choices are carved into the wood as surely as the words are carved into the stone. My jaw loosens. Time stretches. I want to stay inside this — my hearing confirming the corridor's silence beneath the warmth, the body's quiet certainty that what I built is mine regardless of what any document says.

**But the focus has narrowed too far.** My ears catch it before the thought forms — not a sound, but the absence of certainty that the corridor is still empty. The background monitoring that was running all along sharpens into something pointed. The fine hairs on my forearms lift. If someone entered now, they would see a man studying an inscription with a stillness that belongs to someone who has found something, not someone who is browsing. My gaze lifts from the stone without my spine yielding its height — settling on the shelves, the window, the pattern of light on the floorboards. The inscription sinks into my periphery where it is still mine but no longer written in my posture. My hands move to the nearest book and pull it half an inch from the shelf. Idle browsing. A man alone in a library. My ears hold the door.
